【0†iframe】

# The Rust Reference

【1†[attributes.testing]】
# 【2†Testing attributes】

The following 【3†attributes】 are used for specifying functions for performing tests. Compiling a crate in “test” mode enables building the test functions along with a test harness for executing the tests. Enabling the test mode also enables the 【4†`test` conditional compilation option】.

【5†[attributes.testing.test]】
## 【6†The `test` attribute】

【7†[attributes.testing.test.intro]】

The `test` 【3†attribute】 marks a function to be executed as a test.

> Example
>
>     `#![allow(unused)]
>     fn main() {
>     pub fn add(left: u64, right: u64) -> u64 { left + right }
>     #[test]
>     fn it_works() {
>         let result = add(2, 2);
>         assert_eq!(result, 4);
>     }
>     }`

【8†[attributes.testing.test.syntax]】

The `test` attribute uses the 【9†MetaWord】 syntax.
【10†[attributes.testing.test.allowed-positions]】

Tests

The `test` attribute may only be applied to 【11†free functions】 that are monomorphic, that take no arguments, and where the return type implements the 【12†`Termination`】 trait.

> Note
>
> Some of types that implement the 【12†`Termination`】 trait include:
>
>   * `()`
>   * `Result<T, E> where T: Termination, E: Debug`

【13†[attributes.testing.test.duplicates]】

Only the first use of `test` on a function has effect.
> Note
>
> `rustc` lints against any use following the first. This may become an error in the future.

【14†[attributes.testing.test.stdlib]】

The `test` attribute is exported from the standard library prelude as 【15†`std::prelude::v1::test`】.

【16†[attributes.testing.test.enabled]】

These functions are only compiled when in test mode.

> Note
>
> The test mode is enabled by passing the `--test` argument to `rustc` or using `cargo test`.

【17†[attributes.testing.test.success]】

Tests
The test harness calls the returned value’s 【18†`report`】 method, and classifies the test as passed or failed depending on whether the resulting 【19†`ExitCode`】 represents successful termination. In particular:
  * Tests that return `()` pass as long as they terminate and do not panic.
  * Tests that return a `Result<(), E>` pass as long as they return `Ok(())`.
  * Tests that return `ExitCode::SUCCESS` pass, and tests that return `ExitCode::FAILURE` fail.
  * Tests that do not terminate neither pass nor fail.
> Example
>
>     `#![allow(unused)]
>     fn main() {
>     use std::io;
>     fn setup_the_thing() -> io::Result<i32> { Ok(1) }
>     fn do_the_thing(s: &i32) -> io::Result<()> { Ok(()) }
>     #[test]
>     fn test_the_thing() -> io::Result<()> {
>         let state = setup_the_thing()?; // expected to succeed
>         do_the_thing(&state)?;          // expected to succeed
>         Ok(())
>     }
>     }`

【20†[attributes.testing.ignore]】
## 【21†The `ignore` attribute】

【22†[attributes.testing.ignore.intro]】

The `ignore` 【3†attribute】 can be used with the 【5†`test` attribute】 to tell the test harness to not execute that function as a test.

> Example
>
>     `#![allow(unused)]
>     fn main() {
>     #[test]
>     #[ignore]
>     fn check_thing() {
>         // …
>     }
>     }`

> Note
>
> The `rustc` test harness supports the `--include-ignored` flag to force ignored tests to be run.

【23†[attributes.testing.ignore.syntax]】
The `ignore` attribute uses the 【9†MetaWord】 and 【24†MetaNameValueStr】 syntaxes.

【25†[attributes.testing.ignore.reason]】

The 【24†MetaNameValueStr】 form of the `ignore` attribute provides a way to specify a reason why the test is ignored.

> Example
>
>     `#![allow(unused)]
>     fn main() {
>     #[test]
>     #[ignore = "not yet implemented"]
>     fn mytest() {
>         // …
>     }
>     }`

【26†[attributes.testing.ignore.allowed-positions]】
The `ignore` attribute may only be applied to functions annotated with the `test` attribute.

> Note
>
> `rustc` ignores use in other positions but lints against it. This may become an error in the future.

【27†[attributes.testing.ignore.duplicates]】

Only the first use of `ignore` on a function has effect.

> Note
>
> `rustc` lints against any use following the first. This may become an error in the future.

【28†[attributes.testing.ignore.behavior]】
Ignored tests are still compiled when in test mode, but they are not executed.

【29†[attributes.testing.should_panic]】
## 【30†The `should_panic` attribute】

【31†[attributes.testing.should_panic.intro]】

The `should_panic` 【3†attribute】 causes a test to pass only if the 【5†test function】 to which the attribute is applied panics.

> Example
>
>     `#![allow(unused)]
>     fn main() {
>     #[test]
>     #[should_panic(expected = "values don't match")]
>     fn mytest() {
>         assert_eq!(1, 2, "values don't match");
>     }
>     }`

【32†[attributes.testing.should_panic.syntax]】

Tests
The `should_panic` attribute has these forms:

  * 【9†MetaWord】

> Example
>
>     `#![allow(unused)]
>     fn main() {
>     #[test]
>     #[should_panic]
>     fn mytest() { panic!("error: some message, and more"); }
>     }`

  * 【24†MetaNameValueStr】 — The given string must appear within the panic message for the test to pass.
> Example
>
>     `#![allow(unused)]
>     fn main() {
>     #[test]
>     #[should_panic = "some message"]
>     fn mytest() { panic!("error: some message, and more"); }
>     }`

  * 【33†MetaListNameValueStr】 — As with the 【24†MetaNameValueStr】 syntax, the given string must appear within the panic message.

> Example
>
>     `#![allow(unused)]
>     fn main() {
>     #[test]
>     #[should_panic(expected = "some message")]
>     fn mytest() { panic!("error: some message, and more"); }
>     }`
【34†[attributes.testing.should_panic.allowed-positions]】

The `should_panic` attribute may only be applied to functions annotated with the `test` attribute.

> Note
>
> `rustc` ignores use in other positions but lints against it. This may become an error in the future.

【35†[attributes.testing.should_panic.duplicates]】

Only the first use of `should_panic` on a function has effect.
> Note
>
> `rustc` lints against any use following the first with a future-compatibility warning. This may become an error in the future.

【36†[attributes.testing.should_panic.expected]】

Tests

When the 【24†MetaNameValueStr】 form or the 【33†MetaListNameValueStr】 form with the `expected` key is used, the given string must appear somewhere within the panic message for the test to pass.

【37†[attributes.testing.should_panic.return]】

The return type of the test function must be `()`.
